title: John 1:1 and the Pre-existence of Christ

keyTerms.d: The verb of John 1:1 is the imperfect ēn (“was”), not the aorist egeneto (“came to be”) that John uses of created things in verse 3 and of John the Baptist in verse 6. The Word does not come into being at the beginning; the Word already is when the beginning happens. This is the grammar of eternal pre-existence.

The preposition pros with the accusative suggests relationship and orientation — the Word is face-to-face with God, personally distinct from the Father. Whatever John means in the third clause, he does not mean that the Word simply is the Father. There are two who can be “with” one another.

In clause three, theos (“God”) has no article and stands before the verb: kai theos ēn ho logos. Because ho logos (“the Word”) carries the article it is the subject, and the anarthrous theos is the predicate — so the sense is “and the Word was God.”

Anarthrous predicate nouns preceding the verb usually carry a qualitative force — they describe the nature of the subject. In John 1:1c theos is neither definite nor indefinite but qualitative. The grammar by itself ascribes the kind — deity as to nature; it is the monotheism of the same Gospel, which knows only one divine nature and no gradations within the Godhead, that rules out any lesser or second-rank deity. To call theos qualitative is not to say the Word is “sort of” God, or divine by degree, or a step below the Father.

A pattern about definiteness: definite predicate nouns that precede the verb usually lack the article. It was soon misapplied in reverse — as if an anarthrous predicate before the verb must therefore be definite, proving theos means “the God.” That overreaches; the rule does not run backward. The qualitative reading comes from later, more careful work on the construction, not from this rule.

In his incarnate mission the Son willingly submits to the Father’s will — an economic/functional ordering of roles. Not that the Son is lesser in being, made, or later than the Father (Arianism): he is homoousios — co-equal and co-eternal, sharing one divine nature. The Father is greater in position, within the incarnate mission, not greater in deity.

“Of one substance” — the same divine essence — with the Father: the word the Nicene fathers used to confess the Son. The grammarian’s reading of John 1:1c and the bishops’ word for the creed name the same reality; and it is that convergence, not the missing article, that finally carries the verse.

Monogenēs (“only-begotten”) is silence rather than support for a created Son: even read as “only-begotten,” the word names no beginning — and a begetting with no beginning is not a making: begotten, not made, as Nicaea confesses. That is the distinction the Nicene fathers drew in so many words.

derive.q: John uses egeneto (“came to be”) for created things in verse 3, but ēn (“was”) for the Word in verse 1 — so the Word…?
derive.ans: already is when the beginning happens
derive.why: The Word does not come into being at the beginning; the Word already is when the beginning happens. This is the grammar of eternal pre-existence; and with verse 3 — a creature cannot be the agent through whom “all things were made” without being made through himself — it rules out a beginning to the Word’s existence, which is precisely what Arianism requires.

derive.q: Clause two says the Word was “with God” (pros ton theon) — so whatever clause three means, it cannot mean…?
derive.ans: that the Word simply is the Father
derive.why: The preposition pros with the accusative suggests relationship and orientation — the Word is face-to-face with God, personally distinct from the Father. There are two who can be “with” one another. The orthodox reading does not collapse the tension with clause three; it confesses it.

derive.q: In kai theos ēn ho logos, “the Word” carries the article and “God” does not, and stands before the verb — so which is the subject?
derive.ans: the Word — theos is the predicate
derive.why: Word for word the order runs “and—God—was—the—Word,” but because ho logos (“the Word”) carries the article it is the subject, and the anarthrous theos is the predicate — so the sense is “and the Word was God.”

derive.q: With the article on theos, John would have made the Word identical to the Father; meaning “a god,” he would have made the Word a lesser divine being. What he actually wrote says…?
derive.ans: the Word shares the very nature of God without being the person of the Father
derive.why: Had John written ho theos ēn ho logos, he would have said the Word is identical to the Father — the heresy later called modalism. Had he intended the indefinite “a god,” he would have made the Word a lesser divine being — a kind of polytheism. What John actually wrote threads the needle. To call theos qualitative is not to say the Word is “sort of” God: the grammar by itself ascribes the kind — deity as to nature; it is the monotheism of the same Gospel, which knows only one divine nature and no gradations within the Godhead, that rules out any lesser or second-rank deity.

derive.q: “All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made” (1:3) — so the Word is…?
derive.ans: not among the made things — on the Creator’s side of the line
derive.why: The maker of all made things is not among the made things: a creature cannot be the agent through whom “all things were made” without being made through himself. The Word is on the Creator’s side of the line between Creator and creation.

derive.q: The NWT renders the article-less theos of 1:18 “the only-begotten god,” lower case, in the same verse in which it prints “God” of the Father, where the Greek is equally without the article — so the “a god” rendering is…?
derive.ans: theology-driven rather than rule-driven (but this alone decides no single verse)
derive.why: The article is constant across the two; the referent is not. Witnesses reply that context — not a mechanical rule — should govern each verse; that principle is true, and it is ours too. So this point does not by itself decide the meaning of any single verse. Its only force is the limited but real one of showing that the “a god” rendering is theology-driven rather than rule-driven.

honestState.p1: On the grammar, there is a broad consensus that theos in 1:1c is qualitative, not indefinite; read with the monotheism of the same Gospel, that is the full deity of the Word. The minority who defend “a god” are concentrated outside the academic mainstream. On the history, the field is more divided: the dating and development of Christology is genuinely contested terrain. But those disagreements are downstream of this sentence rather than about it.
honestState.fairness: Some on our own side have claimed too much. Colwell’s rule was soon misapplied in reverse — as if an anarthrous predicate before the verb must therefore be definite — and many scholars who love the orthodox conclusion have leaned on it too hard. And the argument from the NWT’s rendering of the article-less theos at 1:6, 1:12 and 1:13 as “God” is narrower than polemics often claim: those are anarthrous genitives, not preverbal predicate nominatives, so they are not the identical construction.
honestState.verdict: John 1:1, carefully read, establishes that this author, writing this Gospel, confesses the Word as eternally pre-existent, personally distinct from the Father, and fully sharing the divine nature — and that he sees the man Jesus as that Word enfleshed, the one the church confesses as fully God and fully man, two natures in one person. That is enough to anchor the Nicene confession in the text and to answer both the “a god” and the Arian readings. It does not, by itself, settle how quickly the whole church arrived at this confession, and it is one strand of the New Testament case for Christ’s deity, not the whole of it.

order: John 1:1–3: the Word already was, was with God, was God — and all things were made through him.
If all created things were made through the Word, the Word cannot be a created thing.
Therefore the Word is eternally pre-existent, personally distinct from the Father, and fully sharing the divine nature.

props.t: the agent through whom all things were made
identical to the person of the Father
proved by the missing article alone
a qualitative reading that comes from Colwell’s rule
the entire New Testament case for Christ’s deity

cards.q: State Premise 1 — the three clauses of John 1:1, and verse 3.
cards.a: In the beginning the Word already was (eternal, not created); the Word was with God (a distinct person, not collapsed into the Father); and the Word was God (fully divine in nature). And all things were made through him.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and why it holds.
cards.a: If absolutely all created things were made through the Word, the Word himself cannot be a created thing — a creature cannot be the agent through whom “all things were made” without being made through himself. The maker of all made things is not among the made things.

cards.q: What does the argument establish — and what does it not, by itself, settle?
cards.a: That this author confesses the Word as eternally pre-existent, personally distinct from the Father, and fully sharing the divine nature — and the man Jesus as that Word enfleshed, fully God and fully man. It does not, by itself, settle how quickly the whole church arrived at this confession; and it is one strand of the New Testament case, not the whole of it.

cards.q: What does the contrast between ēn and egeneto show?
cards.a: Created things came to be (egeneto); the Word simply was (ēn). The Word does not come into being at the beginning; the Word already is when the beginning happens — the grammar of eternal pre-existence; taken with verse 3, it rules out a beginning to the Word’s existence.

cards.q: What does “with God” (pros ton theon) guard against?
cards.a: Collapsing the Word into the Father. Pros with the accusative suggests relationship and orientation — face-to-face with God, personally distinct. Whatever the third clause means, it does not mean the Word simply is the Father: there are two who can be “with” one another.

cards.q: In kai theos ēn ho logos, how do you know which word is the subject?
cards.a: The subject carries the article: ho logos (“the Word”) has it, so it is the subject, and the article-less theos standing before the verb is the predicate — so the sense is “and the Word was God.”

cards.q: What does it mean to call theos “qualitative” — and what does it not mean?
cards.a: It describes the nature of the subject: the Word has the full nature of deity, while remaining personally distinct from the Father. It does not mean “sort of” God, divine by degree, or a step below the Father. The grammar by itself ascribes the kind; it is the monotheism of the same Gospel, which knows only one divine nature and no gradations within the Godhead, that rules out any lesser deity.

cards.q: What is the rule about definite predicate nouns often cited here — and how is it misapplied?
cards.a: It observes that definite predicate nouns preceding the verb usually lack the article. It is misapplied in reverse — as if an article-less predicate before the verb must therefore be definite, proving theos means “the God.” The rule does not run backward, and it is not the source of the qualitative reading.

cards.q: Reply to: the Greek has no article, so it says “a god.”
cards.a: The absence of the article does not by itself make a noun indefinite; this construction points to quality, not indefiniteness. The grammar ascribes the kind; the monotheism of the same Gospel, which knows only one divine nature and no gradations within the Godhead, rules out any lesser deity. The technical form of the argument takes a qualitative reading and then translates it indefinitely — a further step, and one the study’s own paraphrase does not take. The article-less theos does mark a distinction — the Word is not the Father — but between two persons sharing one divine nature, not between God and a demigod.

cards.q: What can honestly be said about how the NWT renders article-less theos elsewhere in John 1 — and what are its limits?
cards.a: At 1:6, 1:12 and 1:13 it renders article-less theos “God” — but those are genitives, not preverbal predicate nominatives, so not the identical construction. The sharper case is 1:18: “the only-begotten god,” lower case, beside “God” for the Father, though the Greek text the NWT translates lacks the article at both. It shows the “a god” rendering is theology-driven, not rule-driven; it does not by itself decide any single verse.

cards.q: Reply to: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28) shows the Word is a lesser, derived god.
cards.a: The Son’s subordination in John is functional (in his role and incarnation), not ontological (in his nature). The words are spoken by the Son who has taken “the form of a servant,” having been “in the form of God” (Philippians 2:6–7): the Father is greater in position, within the incarnate mission, not greater in deity. The Son is not lesser in being, made, or later than the Father — co-equal and co-eternal, sharing one divine nature.

cards.q: Does “only-begotten” (monogenēs) imply the Son was made?
cards.a: No — it is silence rather than support. Even read as “only-begotten,” the word names no beginning — and a begetting with no beginning is not a making: begotten, not made, as Nicaea confesses. One who shares the very nature of God is not a creature.

obj.q: There is no definite article before theos in the last clause, but there is one before “God” in clause two. So the honest translation is “the Word was a god” — which keeps the Father and the Word distinct.
obj.model: The absence of the article does not by itself make a noun indefinite, and the construction here — an article-less predicate before the verb — points to quality, not indefiniteness: it says what the Word is. Even the technical form of your argument, which cites the very study of this construction that we do, takes a qualitative reading and then translates it indefinitely — a further step the study’s own paraphrase does not take; its preferred sense is that the Word “had the same nature as God.” The great majority of Greek scholars reject “a god” as the best reading. The article-less theos does mark a distinction — and it is the historic faith’s own confession: the Word is not the Father. The grammar ascribes the kind; the monotheism of the same Gospel, which knows only one divine nature and no gradations within the Godhead, rules out any lesser deity. But the distinction John draws is between two persons sharing one divine nature, not between God and a demigod. The weight of the case is carried by the construction and by the monotheistic, creation-saturated context of John 1, which is what rules “a god” out. That reading is a mistake, and one who shares the very nature of God is not a creature. And the creation-saturated context closes the case: if all things were made through the Word, the Word is not among the made things.

obj.q: The Word is pre-existent and exalted above all creatures, but derived — divine in a lesser sense. Jesus himself says “the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), and the whole of John has the Son sent and obeying.
obj.model: The Son’s subordination in John is functional — in his role and incarnation — not ontological, in his nature: in his incarnate mission the Son willingly submits to the Father’s will, which is not to say he is lesser in being, made, or later than the Father. “The Father is greater than I” is spoken by the Son who has, in Paul’s words, taken “the form of a servant,” having been “in the form of God” (Philippians 2:6–7); the Father is greater in position, within the incarnate mission, not greater in deity. And the text rules out the derived reading: the verb ēn in 1:1 — eternal “was,” not created “came to be” — rules out a beginning to the Word’s existence, which is precisely what that reading requires; and a creature cannot be the agent through whom “all things were made” (1:3) without being made through himself. The Son is homoousios — co-equal and co-eternal with the Father, sharing one divine nature. So the Arian reading does not hold.

obj.q: Jewish literature personifies God’s word and wisdom poetically. John is doing theology by metaphor, not describing a person.
obj.model: John did not coin Logos in a vacuum: in the Hebrew Scriptures God’s word creates (“by the word of the LORD the heavens were made,” Psalm 33:6) and his Wisdom is personified as present at creation. But John takes this rich vocabulary and does something no Jewish writer had done. Personifications do not become flesh: John says this Word “became flesh” (1:14), a particular man, in history — and brings his Gospel to its climax with Thomas calling him “my Lord and my God” (20:28). And the Word is not merely a figure of speech beside God: he is “with God,” face-to-face, personally distinct. The categories were Jewish; the claim was new.

obj.q: Proverbs 8:22 has Wisdom say the LORD “created me” at the beginning. If the Word is Wisdom, the Word is a creature — exactly as Arius said.
obj.model: Proverbs is poetry, and John does not quote it — he writes “in the beginning” to echo Genesis 1, where the only actor is God. Whatever Proverbs’ poetry means, John’s prose says the Word made everything that was made: “without him was not any thing made that was made” (1:3). And John’s verbs keep the Word out of the created category: created things came to be, but the Word already was when the beginning happened, and everything that was made was made through him. Together these rule out a beginning to the Word’s existence, precisely what the Arian reading requires. So Proverbs 8 does not make the Word a creature.

unseen.q: The study you lean on pairs John 1:1 with Mark 15:39, where the centurion says Jesus was “Son of God” in the very same construction — and a Roman soldier was not confessing full deity. So the construction can’t give you deity in John 1:1 either.
unseen.model: Grant the first half: the parallel is grammatical, not theological — Mark 15:39 is a centurion’s confession using the title “Son of God,” not itself a claim to full deity. But that is exactly what the pairing shows: grammatically the two are the same construction, and Harner reads both qualitatively — the stress falls on the nature the predicate ascribes, not on whether it should be counted “a” son or “the” son. The construction ordinarily says what the subject is; it does not set the content of the predicate. In John 1:1c the predicate is theos. The grammar by itself ascribes the kind — deity as to nature; it is the monotheism of the same Gospel, which knows only one divine nature and no gradations within the Godhead, that rules out any lesser or second-rank deity. Put the two together and what is left is the full divine nature, without remainder, with the predicate withholding only the personal identity of the Father. So the reading that makes the Word fully God as to nature is not an expedient invented to rescue a single verse; it is how the Greek construction regularly works — and it is that convergence, not the missing article, that finally carries the verse.
